content:
Someone wants to join your Core Group, and they tell you why. That story matters. It is also unfinished. Right Reasons is one of the five interview criteria, and it asks whether they are joining for a healthy motive. You cannot answer that from the first sentence they offer.

This article is for the conversation, not for a verdict. Ask about their hopes, their prior church experience, and their willingness to share the work. A concerning answer is a reason to listen further. It is not proof of a hidden motive. An invitation to a Vision Meeting is not a Core Group commitment. If a judgment is needed, you make it. The software does not.

---

## The first story is not the verdict

People arrive with mixed reasons. One person feels called to help start a church. Another is tired of the church they attend. Another wants friends, a role, or a way out of a fight. "I am unhappy where I am" may mean they have prayed and want a place to serve. It may mean they are leaving a conflict they have not faced. The opening line does not tell you which.

[Growing Your Core Group](/wiki/core-group/building-your-core-group/growing-your-core-group) already lists people unhappy at their current church among the people you may invite. Invite them. Talk with them. The invitation is not a commitment, and the unhappiness is not a verdict.

[The 5 Interview Criteria](/wiki/frameworks/the-5-interview-criteria) names healthy motives and warning signs under Right Reasons. Keep both. A warning sign tells you what to ask next. It does not finish the interview. [Interviewing for Fit](/wiki/core-group/follow-up/interviewing-for-fit) calls this mutual discernment. Either of you can say not now.

<Callout type="insight">
  A clean-sounding reason can still hide a mismatch. A messy reason can still belong to someone who will serve faithfully. The words open the interview. They are not the result.
</Callout>

---

## Ask what they hope for

Start with what they want, not with what you fear.

- What are you hoping this church will be?
- What stayed with you after the Vision Meeting?
- What would you hate to miss if you never joined?
- What do you hope to receive here, and what do you hope to give?

Healthy motives sound like a calling to this work, a desire to serve, and a real yes to the vision you hold. Listen for those. Then test them against the work, not against your preferred phrasing.

Also listen for a story that is only about what they will get. That is a warning sign, not a label you apply after one hopeful sentence. Ask what they expect from the Core Group, from the Senior Pastor, and from the first year. Then name the actual work: invitation, service, giving, and staying when the week is ordinary.

If the hope is mostly "I want to be around good people," do not sneer. Ask what they will contribute. Community is a gift. A Core Group commitment is also a job.

---

## Ask about the church they are leaving

Their last church is context. It is not a charge.

- What was good there?
- What became hard?
- How are you leaving, or how did you leave?
- Is there a conversation you still owe someone there?

The interview criteria connect escape from conflict, pursuit of influence, and consumer expectations with poor fit. Use those patterns as doors, not as findings.

| What you heard | What to ask next |
| --- | --- |
| Leaving a conflict | What happened, what they own, and what is still open |
| A role, a title, or influence | What work they will do if no role is open |
| Loneliness, hurt, or a search for any community | What care they need now, and what work they can carry |

None of those answers proves a hidden motive. Leaving a harmful setting is not an automatic no, and it is not an automatic yes. A person may need a church and still not be ready for this commitment. Ask which one you are hearing.

Do not put their old church on trial. You are learning whether they can walk with this Core Group without bringing an unfinished fight with them.

They say, "I just need a church that is not a mess. My last one blew up." You do not answer, "So you are running." You say, "That sounds painful. What happened, and what do you hope will be different here? This is a building season, not a finished church. What part of the work will you carry?"

<Callout type="warning">
  Do not treat loneliness, church hurt, or a hard exit as proof of a bad motive. Those stories are reasons to ask more. They are not a shortcut to yes or to no.
</Callout>

---

## Ask whether they will share the work

Right reasons show up when the work is ordinary.

- What part of inviting, serving, and staying fits your life now?
- Where have you served when no one noticed?
- What would you rather not do?
- If no platform is open for a while, are you still glad to be here?

A person who will set up chairs or invite friends is showing a different posture than a person who wants to direct the plant. Neither answer closes the case. The second one means you keep talking. Growing the Core Group belongs to the whole group. It is not a chair waiting for a new leader.

They say, "I have led worship for years. I assume I would lead here." Thank them, then ask, "That role may not be open. What else would you be glad to do, and how would you feel if it went to someone else?" The answer tells you more than the resume.

Season of life still belongs in the wider interview. A healthy reason with no margin is a timing issue. "Not now" is not a judgment of character, calling, or spiritual health.

If a spouse or someone else in the household is carrying the interest, ask the quieter person what they want. A divided yes needs another conversation. It does not prove that anyone is insincere.

---

## Keep listening before you answer

A concerning answer means you have more to ask. It does not mean you have found a hidden motive. Repeat what you heard. Ask whether you got it right.

<Callout type="tip">
  Write what they said, what you asked next, and what you still do not know. Notes help the next conversation. They are not a score, and they are not a diagnosis.
</Callout>

A second meeting is not drift. It is how you hear the rest before you answer.

You can meet again. You can say this commitment is not right now. You can point someone toward care, another church, or the next Vision Meeting. Do that when you can name what you heard and they recognize it. Do not skip the questions. Do not wait until every uneasy feeling disappears. Unease is a prompt. A named mismatch is something you can say out loud.

Try this: "I heard that you want a leadership role before you have served with us, and that other ways of joining do not interest you. Did I hear that right?" If they confirm it, you have a stated mismatch, not a theory about their heart. Wait on the commitment. Keep the relationship if they want it. Do not punish them for telling you the truth.

If the reason fits, and the other four criteria fit, ask them to join. Do not leave a suitable person uninvited because you wanted a cleaner story.

---

## What you record, and what you do not

After the conversation, you may record a human judgment on Right Reasons: pass, fail, or concern, with notes and a next step. Fail means you can name a real mismatch, not that you dislike their story. Concern means keep talking, or wait before you ask for commitment. Pass means the reason fits. You still weigh maturity, gifts, chemistry, and season of life before you treat them as ready.

Everyfield stores that record if you enter it. It does not make the judgment. The software never judges calling, character, fitness, or spiritual health. It does not certify a person to join, and it does not block a person because of a phrase in a note.

If you are unsure, record concern and set the next conversation. Do not guess a fail to look discerning. Do not guess a pass to fill the group.

---

## Mistakes that skip the conversation

- Treating the first story as a verdict.
- Using the warning table as a list of banned motives.
- Confusing a Vision Meeting invitation with a Core Group commitment.
- Skipping the other four criteria because the reason sounded good.
- Waiting forever because you never asked the next question.
- Offering a role to quiet your own doubt about their motive.

<Callout type="scripture">
  *"He who responds with a word before he hears, It is folly and shame to him."* — Proverbs 18:13 (LSB)
</Callout>

Hear them first. Then you can invite, wait, or say not now.

title: Healthy and Unhealthy Reasons to Join

sources.claim: A response that comes before hearing is called folly. The article uses this as the reason to ask before treating a motive as known.

claim_check.notes: Owner review by Sebastian; no model review per his 2026-10-26 instruction.

rulings: Bryan ruled R4 = Option A: "Questions before conclusions" (2026-10-26 1:31 PM ET).
Wording call: kept the backlog title Healthy and Unhealthy Reasons to Join. The ruling governs the method, not the title.

Wording call: published warning signs (escape from conflict, pursuit of influence, consumer expectations) are named as questions to ask next, not as proof of a hidden motive. That keeps Option A consistent with The 5 Interview Criteria and Interviewing for Fit without copying their verdict tone.
Wording call: invitation and commitment stay distinct, matching Growing Your Core Group, which already lists people unhappy at their current church as possible invitees.

Wording call: deferral is an existing interview outcome after a named, recognized mismatch, not a rule that concerns must be resolved before anyone joins. Bryan chose questions before conclusions, not Option B.
Wording call: did not cite Stetzer and Rogers in the article or in sources. The book has no fetchable URL and its text must not be copied. Named only in the PR body as background.
Wording call: no SBC or Send Network specifics, and no claim that Everyfield judges calling, character, fitness, or spiritual health.
